source_text:
12 πῶς τὸν
ἀκατάληπτον καὶ ἀνεκδιήγητον καὶ ἀπερινόητον ἀπερίγραφόν τε γράφειν λέγει τις,

ον οὐκ ι σχυσε Μωυσῆς ἀτενίσαι; 13 φασίν τινες οτι ἐπειδὴ τέλειος ανθρωπος
ἐγένετο ἐκ Μαρίας τῆς ἀειπαρθένου, διὰ τοῦτο ανθρωπον αὐτὸν ποιοῦμεν. 14 καὶ διὰ
τοῦτο ἐνηνθρώπησεν, ινα τὸν ἀκατάληπτον δι' ου τὰ πάντα ἐγένετο, διὰ χειρῶν σου
γράψαι δυνηθῇς; 15 οὐκοῦν οὐκ εστιν ομοιος τοῦ πατρὸς οὐδὲ ζωοποιεῖ τοὺς
νεκρούς; 16 ποῦ σοι διέταξε ταῦτα ἐλθὼν ἐπὶ γῆς, ποιῆσαι ομοιον αὐτῷ καὶ
προσκυνεῖν καὶ ὁρᾶν; 17 αυ τη ἡ διάταξις τοῦ πονηροῦ ἐστιν, ινα καταφρονήσῃς
θεοῦ. 18 ὁ θεὸς γὰρ ἐν πάσῃ τῇ παλαιᾷ καὶ καινῇ ταῦτα ἀναιρεῖ, ἀκριβῶς λέγων·
«κύριον τὸν θεὸν προσκυνήσεις καὶ αὐτῷ μόνῳ λατρεύσεις».
thought_title: No one can depict the incomprehensible Christ
orientation: Epiphanius is closing his treatise by attacking the opponents' claim that the incarnate Christ can be depicted, arguing that the command to make such images comes from the evil one, not from God.
pass_a_gloss: How does someone say to depict the incomprehensible and inexpressible and inconceivable and not able to be encompassed or depicted one, whom Moses was not strong enough to gaze upon? Some say that since a perfect human being came into being from Mary the ever-virgin, for this reason we make him a human being. And for this reason did he become incarnate, so that the incomprehensible one through whom all things came into being might be able to be depicted by your hands? Therefore is he not like the Father, and does he not give life to the dead? Where did he command you these things when he came upon earth, to make a likeness of him and to worship and to see? This is the command of the evil one, so that you might despise God. For God in all the old and new covenant abolishes these things, saying precisely: "You shall worship the Lord your God and him alone shall you serve."

choices.why: Glossary term for what is beyond human grasp, applied to Christ even after the incarnation.
Glossary term for what cannot be contained or delimited by a visual form.
Glossary term for the act that belongs to God alone.
Refers to the devil, the source of the command to make images.
Refers to the Old and New Testaments; the adjective pair functions substantivally for the two covenants.

bible_refs.note: κύριον τὸν θεὸν προσκυνήσεις καὶ αὐτῷ μόνῳ λατρεύσεις

pass_b_english: How can anyone claim to paint the incomprehensible, the inexpressible, the inconceivable, the one who cannot be encompassed or depicted—the one Moses could not even gaze upon? Some say, "Since he became a perfect human being from Mary the ever-virgin, that is why we make him as a human being." And did he become incarnate for this reason—so that you could paint with your hands the incomprehensible one through whom all things were made? Then is he not like the Father, and does he not give life to the dead? Where did he command you, when he came to earth, to make something like him and to worship it and gaze upon it? This command is from the evil one, so that you would despise God. For God abolishes these things in all the Old and New Testaments, saying precisely: "You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve" (Deuteronomy 6:13).

problems.quote: Then is he not like the Father, and does he not give life to the dead?
problems.source_quote: οὐκοῦν οὐκ ἔστιν ὅμοιος τοῦ πατρὸς οὐδὲ ζωοποιεῖ τοὺς νεκρούς;
problems.why: The Greek asks rhetorically whether Christ IS like the Father and DOES give life to the dead (both positive). English 'not like' and 'does he not give life' makes it a double negative confusion, flipping the rhetorical force.
problems.fix: Then is he not like the Father, and does he not give life to the dead?
problems.ruling: οὐκοῦν οὐκ ἔστιν ὅμοιος...οὐδὲ ζωοποιεῖ expects affirmative answers; English negative questions flip rhetorical force.

problems.quote: in all the old and new covenant
problems.why: τῇ παλαιᾷ καινῇ refers to 'the old and new [Testament/scripture]', not 'covenant' singular. The phrase means 'in all the Old and New [Testaments]'.
problems.fix: in all the Old and New Testaments
problems.ruling: παλαιᾷ καιν�ῇ with πάσῃ implies Old and New Testaments/scriptures; singular 'covenant' misleads readers.

problems.quote: Then is he not like the Father, and does he not give life to the dead?
problems.source_quote: οὐκοῦν οὐκ εστιν ομοιος τοῦ πατρὸς οὐδὲ ζωοποιεῖ τοὺς νεκρούς;
problems.why: Greek asks if he is NOT like the Father and does NOT give life; English flips to positive questions.
problems.fix: Then is he not unlike the Father, and does he not fail to give life to the dead?
problems.ruling: Greek οὐκ εστιν + οὐδὲ expects affirmative answer; English 'is he not' correctly renders negative questions.

edits.old: Then is he not like the Father, and does he not give life to the dead?
edits.new: Then is he not unlike the Father, and does he not fail to give life to the dead?

fixed: The modality problem was real: the Greek asks whether he is not like the Father and does not give life to the dead, so the English was corrected to preserve the negative questions.

problems.quote: Then is he not unlike the Father, and does he not fail to give life to the dead?
problems.source_quote: οὐκοῦν οὐκ εστιν ομοιος τοῦ πατρὸς οὐδὲ ζωοποιεῖ τοὺς νεκρούς;
problems.why: Rhetorical question expecting 'yes he IS like the Father' flipped to 'is he not unlike' = 'he is unlike'. Sense inverted.
problems.fix: Then is he not like the Father, and does he not give life to the dead?
problems.ruling: οὐκ εστιν ομοιος = 'is he not like?' expects yes; 'is he not unlike' inverts to 'he is unlike', changing meaning.

problems.fix: Gloss as 'not able to be encompassed or depicted'.

last_rejected.quote: Some say, "Since he became a perfect human being from Mary the ever-virgin, that is why we make him as a human being."
last_rejected.source_quote: φασίν τινες οτι ἐπειδὴ τέλειος ανθρωπος ἐγένετο ἐκ Μαρίας τῆς ἀειπαρθένου, διὰ τοῦτο ανθρωπον αὐτὸν ποιοῦμεν
last_rejected.why: The English puts the opponents' words in quotation marks and first person 'we', but the source has φασίν τινες with indirect statement (ὅτι... ποιοῦμεν). The 'we' in the source is the opponents speaking in their own voice, which the English captures. However, the English adds quotation marks making it direct speech, which is a stylistic choice. The content is accurate. Actually, checking more carefully: the source has the opponents speaking in first person plural (ποιοῦμεν = 'we make'), so direct quotation is justified. No error.
last_rejected.ruling: ποιοῦμεν is first person plural; opponents speak in own voice. Quotation marks justified. Content accurate.

last_rejected.quote: And did he become incarnate for this reason—so that you could paint with your hands the incomprehensible one through whom all things were made?
last_rejected.source_quote: καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἐνηνθρώπησεν, ινα τὸν ἀκατάληπτον δι' ου τὰ πάντα ἐγένετο, διὰ χειρῶν σου γράψαι δυνηθῇς;
last_rejected.why: The English adds 'And did he become incarnate' with interrogative 'did', making it a rhetorical question expecting 'no'. But the Greek καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἐνηνθρώπησεν is a declarative statement ('and for this reason he became incarnate') followed by ἵνα... δυνηθῇς ('so that you could...'), with the whole thing being a sarcastic question. The English 'And did he become incarnate' changes the force—it's not asking whether he became incarnate, but assuming it and asking whether the purpose was painting. Actually, re-reading: the Greek structure is καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἐνηνθρώπησεν, ἵνα...; which is indeed a rhetorical question. The English captures this. No error.
last_rejected.ruling: καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἐνηνθρώπησεν, ἵνα...; is a rhetorical question. English interrogative 'did' captures the force.

last_rejected.quote: does he not give life to the dead
last_rejected.why: The Greek has οὐδέ (nor/neither), continuing the negative: 'he is not like the Father, nor does he give life to the dead.' The English 'and does he not give life to the dead' with 'not' makes this a separate question with its own negative, which changes the syntax but not necessarily the sense—both are rhetorical questions expecting 'no, of course he does give life.' However, the Greek structure is 'is he not like... nor does he give life' while English is 'is he not like... and does he not give life.' The force is preserved. No error.
last_rejected.ruling: οὐδὲ continues negative rhetorical question; 'and does he not' preserves the same force and meaning.

last_rejected.quote: so that you would despise God
last_rejected.why: The English 'you would despise God' for ἵνα καταφρονήσῃς θεοῦ. The subjunctive with ἵνα here expresses purpose: 'so that you may despise God' or 'to the end that you despise God.' 'Would' adds a conditional or habitual sense not in the Greek. However, in rhetorical contexts, 'would' can express the intended result. This is minor at most.
last_rejected.ruling: ἵνα with subjunctive expresses purpose; 'would' can render intended result in English. Normal range, not an error.
